QUESTION:
Which other drugs interact with Lisinopril?

RESPONSE:
Short answer: the excerpt you've given me (Indications and Usage, Dosage and Administration) does not include the DRUG INTERACTIONS section of the lisinopril/hydrochlorothiazide label, so I can't quote specific interaction language from it. The only interaction-related point in the text provided is that adding lisinopril "blunted the hypokalemia normally seen with diuretics" — i.e., the ACE inhibitor raises potassium while the thiazide lowers it.

For general awareness (not from this excerpt — please verify against the full prescribing information):

• Potassium supplements, potassium-containing salt substitutes, and potassium-sparing diuretics (spironolactone, eplerenone, amiloride, triamterene) — risk of hyperkalemia.
• Other agents blocking the renin-angiotensin system: ARBs (e.g., valsartan) and aliskiren — dual blockade increases hypotension, hyperkalemia, and renal impairment; aliskiren is contraindicated in patients with diabetes and generally avoided with renal impairment.
• Neprilysin inhibitors (sacubitril/valsartan) and racecadotril — contraindicated/avoid within 36 hours because of angioedema risk; mTOR inhibitors (sirolimus, everolimus) and DPP-4 inhibitors may also raise angioedema risk.
• NSAIDs, including COX-2 inhibitors — reduced antihypertensive effect and risk of acute renal deterioration, especially in elderly, volume-depleted, or renally impaired patients.
• Lithium — increased lithium levels and toxicity (both ACE inhibitors and thiazides contribute).
• Diuretics in general — added hypotensive effect, particularly first-dose hypotension in volume-depleted patients.
• Gold (injectable sodium aurothiomalate) — nitritoid reactions reported.
• Antidiabetic agents (insulin, oral agents) — dosage adjustment may be needed; hydrochlorothiazide can raise blood glucose while ACE inhibitors may enhance glucose lowering.
• Hydrochlorothiazide-specific: alcohol/barbiturates/narcotics (orthostatic hypotension), corticosteroids and ACTH (electrolyte depletion), digitalis (hypokalemia-related toxicity), skeletal muscle relaxants, cholestyramine/colestipol (reduced absorption — separate dosing), and other drugs that prolong QT or cause hypokalemia.

Also relevant clinically: monitor renal function and potassium when starting or changing any of these, and tell your prescriber/pharmacist about all prescription, OTC (especially NSAIDs), and herbal products. Please consult the complete package insert or your pharmacist for the authoritative interaction list.
